newsitem.title: USA: HP to add networking for low-cost printers.
newsitem.headline: HP to add networking for low-cost printers.

text.p: Hewlett-Packard Co will on Monday announce plans to provide networking features for lower-cost color printers typically only available on powerful network printers, company managers said.

HP said the new features, due out early in 1997, would enable customers to network its recently introduced HP DeskJet 870 color printer for less than $800, including both the printer and its network server products.
"We see a trend continuing, that more and more personal printers will be attached to networks," said Gary Gubitz, marketing manager for HP's Direct Connect Operation.

"There has been a barrier in that low-end printers have not had the full feature set of the high-end network printers and there has been a price barrier for color in the office," he said. "What we're doing is breaking down both walls, with no compromise on functionality."
HP said it will offer its enhanced JetDirect EX Plus print server, due to be available in February with full DeskJet 870 support, for an estimated street price of around $290.

JetDirect print server users can upgrade existing JetDirect EX Plus print server via a free flash-memory download which is due to be available in January from HP's Network City home page at (http://www.hp.com/go/network_city).
The print server provides sophisticated feedback to customers' screens, such as telling them when paper in the printer is out or a cartridge needs to be replaced.

The DeskJet 870C Professional Series color printer, introduced in August, is a general purpose machine that can print eight pages a minute in black text and half that speed in color. It is available now at street prices of around $500.

HP said that prior to the new networking capability, customers would have needed to spend two to three times the amount to network a black ink laser printer or up to four or five times the price for a networked color laser printer.

"We really believe we're providing the full power of a printing requirement to the user of low cost as well as high performance printers," said Gubitz. "It takes a lot of technology to bring simplicity to this type of business need."
The primary target is to provide greater printer management capabilities for large and small businesses that are bringing personal printers onto computer networks.

HP is aiming the new network capabilities at what it believes is a growing trend of connecting personal printers to networks. The company cited an International Data Corp survey last year which found that 63 percent of network-connected printers were personal printers, with outputs below 12 pages.
Gubitz also pointed to a survey from Sage Research Inc in which 67 percent of respondents said their organizations are printing an increased number of documents in color.

Estimated costs per page for the personal printers also compare favorably with those of HP's LaserJet printers, although the latter are designed and tuned for high volume demands of heavy printing tasks.

A spokesman for HP said estimated per-page printing costs for a DeskJet 870 are three cents for black ink and eight cents for color, compared with 3.5 cents for black ink and 11.5 cents for color on a heavy-duty LaserJet 5 machine.
